identity.title: Triple-BERT: Do We Really Need MARL for Order Dispatch on Ride-Sharing Platforms?

problem.claim: Real-time ride-sharing order dispatch must bundle and match passengers with available vehicles under substantial uncertainty and very large driver/order observation spaces.

gap.claim: Independent MARL methods miss global information and cooperate poorly, while CTDE MARL methods face dimensionality problems for this centralized task.

contributions.claim: Triple-BERT is proposed as a centralized single-agent reinforcement-learning method for large-scale ride-sharing dispatch, built on a TD3 variant with decomposed driver actions.
A BERT-based network uses parameter reuse to limit growth with system scale and attention to model relationships among drivers and orders.
The authors make code, trained parameters, and processed data publicly available.

stated_novelty.claim: The authors distinguish Triple-BERT through centralized single-agent learning, action decomposition, and a BERT-based architecture tailored to large-scale dispatch.

author_reported_evidence.claim: On a real-world Manhattan ride-hailing dataset, the authors report an approximately 11.95% improvement over current state-of-the-art methods.
The authors report a 4.26% increase in served orders and a 22.25% reduction in pickup times.

narrative_sequence.summary: Ride-sharing platforms must dispatch vehicles to passenger requests in uncertain, large-scale environments.
Although dispatch is centralized, MARL is commonly used; independent MARL lacks global information and cooperation, while CTDE faces dimensionality challenges.
Triple-BERT applies centralized single-agent reinforcement learning, decomposes joint actions by driver, and uses a parameter-reusing attention network.
The method is evaluated on Manhattan data, with reported gains in overall performance, served orders, and pickup time; implementation artifacts are released.

source_observation.claim: The abstract links each scaling obstacle to a specific design choice: action decomposition for the action space and parameter reuse plus attention for the observation space.

lessons.interpretation: This provides a compact problem-to-mechanism framing that makes architectural motivation traceable.
lessons.application: For a systems paper, map each stated bottleneck to one named mechanism before presenting aggregate results.
lessons.exception: This framing is unsuitable when the proposed components address overlapping or experimentally inseparable bottlenecks.

unknowns: The abstract does not specify the evaluation metric behind the approximately 11.95% overall improvement, baseline identities, dataset size, or experimental protocol.
The abstract does not report ablations separating action decomposition, parameter reuse, and attention effects.
